I gotta say, the main character is some sort of god in this. He can rebuild an entire engine in under an hour. He can slot in an entire exhaust system as if it's Lego. He can somehow remove the fuel pump without removing anything else on the car. He can determine the exact condition of a set of brake pads through the rims and caliper. Everything is an exact percentage to this man, not "good", "worn" or "needs replacing". Hell, he can replace a timing belt in a matter of seconds. I envy this man.
If you like playing as god, and like working on cars without doing the tedious stuff (or working on literally any French car), then this is the game for you.

In all seriousness, this game helps you learn a lot about the different parts of cars and what they do. I'm no mechanic, I just got a lot of experience on repairing my own cars because they've either been French or just old run down junkboxes on wheels. But this is enjoyable. It's satisfying refurbishing cars, and rebuilding engines. Obviously, it doesn't cover absolutely every aspect. But it will probably give you a much better idea of what the mechanic's telling you when you ever have to take your own car into a garage irl, instead of going "Oh yeah, oh ok, yeah replace whatever tf that is please".

Great game to pass the time, and also learn a bit about cars on the side.
9/10 - Only a couple of crash bugs going into barns, but otherwise a neat game.

The majority of Car Mechanic Simulator '18's content is locked behind grinding, but for good reason. If you're coming in expecting to immediately restore and sell cars for big dosh, guess what, you're gonna to be doing a lot oil changes and brake jobs first because, yes, it is a simulation of you building your talents and reputation as a skilled carsman.

When you first try to repair parts, most will turn to dust because you have big, clumsy hands. You WILL dump oil on to your shop floor because you forgot to drain it before removing the oil pan. You WILL struggle to find the one valve pushrod that's causing the loss of engine power to complete your order unless you pull off the engine heads and investigate. You WILL spend an hour and a half figuring out where and what a fuel pump is.

However, you [i]will[/i] get better, AND you'll unlock tools like compression testers and fuel pressure testers to be able to find the problematic parts, and there-in resides the satisfaction of CMS 2018. You enter as a total neophite, not knowing a thing about how cars work --probably magic-- but as you progress, it starts to make sense. Fuel? Oxygen? Ignition? That's the recipe for [i]GO FAST[/i].

When you've gained enough experience --and levels-- the parts you attempt to repair will more consistantly come out gleaming; factory new. Your garage expands, and now you can repair framework and body parts. The knowledge you've gained spending hours changing filters and swapping leaf springs makes your orders a breeze, and now you have some money to go searching for a ride to make your own. You've found a fastback in a barn. You take it home, and now it's your baby. You pull off the wheels and attend to the suspension; replace the con-rods and pistons with performance parts: Performance plugs, flywheel, ignition wires and filters. Suddenly, the wallflower in the corner is the prom queen at the drag strip because she's doing 0-60 in 4.03 seconds and putting down 491 horsepower on the dyno.

You don't sell her though. You never sell your first. There's many other cars to restore to factory colours with the original rims. Your lady has thick gumballs on the back to soak up the horsepower. The expression of the confidence you've instilled within her.

Maybe it's a 'him'. I call my 310hp I4 Jeep Willys 'Jeeperson Starship'. To each their own.

Pros:

- An immense satisfaction from fixing cars --as opposed to destroying them, [i]Wreckfest[/i]. >:C
- A crash course into how cars work, if that's a thing you want to pursue, or if you want to talk to your dad.
- Level system requires you to put in your dues, but new skills never feel out of reach
- Restoring your first acquisition to factory condition carries a huge sense of accomplishment and pride
- Bangin' soundtrack packed in
- Visually stunning on highest settings, if your video card can handle it

Cons:

- Unless your video card is beef, expect to play at medium or low settings
- No options for racing CPU or other players. Only timed laps are available, and then only on a single circuit
- Faster cars are virtually uncontrollable with mouse & keyboard, so be prepared to switch to a controller
- The drag strip is only available with purchase of the Pontiac DLC

Final Notes:

Like a relationship, you'll start off holding hands and swapping fluids and it'll be confusing; sometimes painful. It will be a grind that might seem mundane and you'll be like 'What am I doing here?" But once you get past that hump, that's when you begin to undersand: That's when CMS opens up and before you know it, that's when you have the wheel in hand, doing sweet burnouts and rimjobs. 9/10

As a mechanic myself, I have a mixed opinion on this game.

If you are wanting to learn car parts, this game is great. The only thing i would say is that some of the parts have different names in different countries, as in. the "Sway bar" is known as the "Anti-Roll bar" In england so just take that in mind.

So what I mean is, this game is very helpful if you want to put names to parts if you are in education of car mechanics however DO NOT expect to learn how to work on cars properly from this game. This game puts it in the simplest form it can be. You cant play a few hours on this game and then go repair a car, all the little fiddly bits and procedures are skipped out of this game and all cars are different whereas these cars within the car seem to follow the same build. 

I'd also like to point out, the mechanic jobs are unrealistic. For example, when replacing Brake Discs/Pads, you should always fit new ones both sides whether its front or rear. Realistically you should never only replace one side because then the brakes will be unbalanced and its dangerous.

This game is a entertaining, a good way to pass time and learn at the same time but like i said, dont expect to go away from this game knowing everything about how cars work because there is A LOT missing, this game is just for fun. You dont have to follow strict guidelines or have to make certain procedures like in reality like changing brake fluid. Personally, as soon as i get into the swing of the game i cant stop. 

But this game is very good if you want to learn the basics and like i said, its a good way to pass time.

I had no business playing a game related to cars. I went into this thinking that the only thing making a car go vroom vroom was an axel. I have learned I was wrong.
And yet, now, I have enjoyed the game immensely; as of writing this I have 100+ hours on this game that I might have otherwise spent on some RPG or sandbox game. Now I get to enjoy the look on my grandfather's face when I ask him about front and rear double wishbone shock absorbers and V8 2carb OHV supercharged engines.

This game has a lot of self-learning. For those just starting, I highly recommend:
1. Do the 'tutorial' (which is more like a quick sandbox) and take apart and put together the cars provided piece by piece. Also, make sure you look at every station around the garage, including the warehouse, the parking garage, the painting room, the two tire-related machines, the oil drainer thingy, the engine remover crane, the engine block stand, the shock assembler mechanism, the battery charger, and the welder and interior fixer-upper. Each will be super useful once you unlock them and you'll want to know they exist and where to find them.
2. When you do a job: when you look at the car's information, pieces that you have identified that need to be replaced have a little grey star next to them. If you click the star, that part will highlight in the car itself. This will help you find it and replace it! Super useful when you have no flipping idea what an Inner Tie Rod is or what it looks like, right? The game never tells you this, unfortunately.
3. When choosing jobs: focus on Brakes, Gearbox, Exhaust, and Body. Engine and Timing take forever. Suspension involves mystery bushing shenanigans. For money, focus on the Gearbox ones. For speed, focus on Exhaust.
Jobs will have little white symbols for what each job will require. Luckily the game eases you into it with one type of job at a time so you can get used to them, until eventually they're flinging everything at you with wild abandon like my brother when he's looking for something in his room.

Everything will become streamlined once you know what you're looking for. I don't even need to highlight anything now. My knowledge has shot up from 'Flintstone car locomotion' to 'v8 custom gearbox tuning' and it feels great.

Don't forget to open your Mystery Cases though. I spent an hour opening my backlog of like 100 of those things. It was the longest surprise party ever.
Didn’t expect to spend hours fixing virtual cars. Weirdly relaxing game

Let's get it out of the way right now: 

No, you will not be granted anything significant of the physics or even that much fruit of your tuning. In fact, the higher power your car has, the more weird it is to drive, even with Racing Slicks. This is Car Mechanic Simulator 2018. This is not Gran Turismo, this is not Fast and the Furious, this is nothing that you'd want as a racer. Racing is not here, except for time trials for the sake of testing your tuning. If you were expecting anything of the like: This is not your game.

Now, for the title, does this provide an excellent view of the parts of the cars and all that stuff that at first may confuse you? Yes. It is good for learning the basics. But, do not expect to be an absolute expert on the matter because there are details, oh so many details, that have gone missing compared to its strongest competitor: Wrench.

If you are looking to have some casual, stress-relieving fun while fixing cars or making Junkyard Rescues? Pick this up. No doubt about it, this may even be right up your alley. But, if you want to get your money's worth, get yourself this game on sale. Do NOT go lower than 50%. I'll explain why: 

DLC feels like at least 50% of this game, and not in a good way. At all. 

The Mercedes-Benz and the Chrysler Packs are neat touches, but they are a little bit too expensive, the latter only bringing you two... Yes, TWO cars! For a regular price of $5 USD. Mercedes is a tad bit more expensive, but the cars are seldom of any interesting value except for the sake of engineering history. 

Let's talk about one of its major, well TWO, major problems: Slow progression, and endgame.

Before the comments fly at me about how this is just a casual game and I shouldn't be too harsh, hear me out: 

This is a simulator, yes. It will NOT cater to everyone and it will certainly cater to a specific kind of audience. I know this. But if you are going to charge us a good amount of dosh for DLC, at least ensure you are getting the content is actually worth the spending.

Yes, licensing is expensive. No, this does not mean it justifies you putting up yet another V8 Engine that is seldom of any difference to the already plentiful V8s that we have. Yes, sometimes even the V8 OHVs of the game, are of similar performance to the Modern V8s! (Provided you tune them right, that is.)

Now, the issues.

Slow Progression: You start with a one-car Garage as you begin your career as a Mechanic. Sounds logical, right? Well, thing is, the EXP gain by this stage can get tedious and slow and you will see yourself burning yourself out quickly at the start. It also does not help that the Tutorial does not help you much, since it only provides you with vague details of items that you must be around Level 30 (correct me if I am wrong, please). By the time, you would have already forgotten about it. Money is seldom a problem, as long as you meet the minimum repairs, you are good.

Endgame: This sounds ridiculous for a casual game, I know. But once you reach Level 30, you are done with the game. Unless you haven't done the story, that is. Once those missions are done, there's nothing else left. This is when, thankfully, the Steam Workshop comes into play. You can count on the community into making some great models for Real Life cars for you to do Junkyard Rescues. Just be careful at the amount of cash being played there. Some of these are mostly there to serve as Cash Farming or even go at ridiculous prices that make you break your own economy to the point where you can reach $10,000,000 with just the repair of a car from a Junkyard, while your initial investment was only of $750,000 or even less. I'm looking at you, McLaren F1 LM.

Now, with the issues out of the way, let's go with the things I really like.

The Music: The EDM Music Radios are actually nice to hear, at least for most of the tracks. Chances are you will enjoy the other genres too. For these songs being Royalty-Free (for the most part), they are not as obnoxious as Super Street: The Game's. This being said, the game allows you to create your own playlist to be played in-game. Just dig in through your game files and you'll see it.

Details and Parts: With so many parts for so many cars this time around, this feels like it has more content and as such, you may feel that the initial price tag is less painful to bear. Especially if you compare it to the earlier entries to the game. Most of the cars that you will find in the base game are recreations of real life cars with altered looks and different names. However, when you dismantle engines, be it your standard I4, Straight 6, or even their recreation of the LS1 Engines... You can clearly see at least a certain degree of detailed work on the parts and other tidbits as you assemble it. (You can even install Racing-Spec Parts, but this requires DLC.) The models may look generic, but you will be presented with plenty to work with. Don't be surprised, this is a rather small studio, after all. Licenses, again, are expensive.

Steam Workshop Support: Perhaps the current most important feature, and even what is keeping this game alive. As stated earlier, reaching the level required for the 3-Slot Garages feels like you have already beaten the game, because even with story missions, you do not feel like you are doing much. Except maybe getting a crate or two with RNG parts with boosted stats from +1 to +5. They share the same parts that they have added in for their cars in the base games and maybe some from the DLC, but other than that? Do not expect much, other than the body panels. Still, it feels great having some JDM being worked on, when they only gave us Mazda.

In short: If you are interested in cars, and know almost next to nothing about them? Get this, it'll shed some light in you, even if just the basics. Maybe even spark an interest in fixing your dad's '69 Camaro? That's your own choice, though.

However, do I recommend the game? Yes. It can be fun if you got absolutely nothing to do. Just note that you should not expect 100% accuracy when fixing these machines, because the lack of detail when compared to Wrench, is meant for it to be accessible for newcomers. 

Get this game on sale, do not go lower than 50%. 

Also, here's the must have DLC, in no particular order: 
- Pagani Pack (So many V12 Car Mods, it's Sebastian Vettel's dream pack.)
- Tuning Pack (It's Free!)
- Rims Pack (Mods need it)
- Garage Customization DLC (Also free!)
- Maserati Remastered Pack (Not exactly a Must-Have, but I have seen mods require it.)

You may ignore the rest, as they all feel redundant and do not exactly bring any significant difference to the game experience whatsoever.

All in all, this is a great game for relaxing. But for the base game being at $20? 

Absolute rip off. Don't pay more than $10 for this.

Good game, pretty car models, but prepare for a grind.
The really fun part (the ability to repair most components and body parts) doesn't start until after you hit lv35. The perk is locked until then. Without that perk all you do is buy parts and un/re screw them.
Perks must also be unlocked in sequence as well as the level lock. 
It ends up being several thousand exp required per level and only 100-150 exp per job fix... you do the math.

You'll need to engage in some sanity-saving tactics:
 - Remember each job is worth 100xp minimum no matter how simple. So do super-simple exhaust only jobs as often as you can and don't feel guilty.
 - Can't find a faulty part because NONE of the testing devices look at it? Abuse the camera zoom to look through things and see what's rusty.
 - Just spent the last hour of real time completely deconstructing an engine because the fault description says "rattle in engine bay"? Remember that could actually mean the damn air filter housing, because **** you. I now know why most actual car mechanics hate people. Simulation successful.
 - "repairing" parts is very random, especially before level 35. Visit the bench regularly to see if RNGeesus simulator decided to give you the chance at fixing a single part.
 - Don't think the more complex fix jobs give lots of exp, they don't. Think of them more like a feat of endurance. (TYVM mystery suspension+engine+brakes rebuild. The two hours was worth that extra 60 exp. NOT.)
 - Don't assume you get to do really satisfying manual grinding/respraying by hand like the intro. Its a mouseclick and done.
 - Appreciate the shiny parts. Mmmm, newly bought grille lensflare...

Not perfect, but fun if you're into cars or want to go from no knowledge to "a little bit of knowledge".

Grease-coated thumbs up.

I know absolutely nothing about cars. Nothing! But way back, i bought this game thinking: 'I like simulators, might as well give this a try." And boy, am I glad I did!!!

You run your own garage, which you slowly but surely upgrade, you level up and can select multiple skill that make the game easier, and the greatest thing to do:  Visit the junkyard (once ya unlocked it), buy a heap of metal that once was a car, and start renovation!!

Only negative thing I think the game has, is the fact that you need to be level 30+ to unlock the tool that fixes the interior of the car. But other than that, give the game a shot! If ya like simulation games, and like renovating things, this is the game for you!!

This game shouldnt have shipped the way it did, lets be honest, but it did. I played it, realised it was buggy as hell and then stopped, figuring i'd leave it a few days and see if a patch was brought out by that time. I came back and not one patch but 4 were released in such a small space of time. Kudos to the developers for the quick patches. I'm very disappointed that people decided to slate the game itself and put horrendous reviews of the game based on just the bugs at day one. You are all entitled to put reviews like that but the reviews stick, the developers should have known this, but months down the line when it's streamlined and bug free those reviews will still be there and it's slightly unfair, especially given the amount of patches in the few days its been.

Personally I feel that this game (after the bug fixes) has improved massively on the last one and while it's true that it can get to feel very samey its a bloody simulator, dont see you moaning about the fact you have to drive from A to B on Euro Trucks now do I? That's the same all through the game. It's added new steps into repairing your car, new tools to use to make this happen and, my favourite, a barn find which you can pick up old classics and restore them to their full glory! There's a skill system that's much better than previous games. Whilst things can still improve with the game over time, i'm more than happy at picking this little gem up for just £14, that#'s nothing for a game nowadays and I feel people forget the amount of hours you can get from this type of game and for what it costs you per hour of gameplay you paid for it. I've only played 4 hours at the moment, that's £3.50 per hour of enjoyment...I'm about to play many more, great value for money!

Having played '21, here some things I did like in this game compared to the sequel:

- repairs: there's no mini-game for every part, you either manage to repair part of it or all of it (or even fail) with a press, no constantly timing when to press... for those of us who manage to end up with large amounts to repair, the mini-game in '21 can be, well... absolutely tedious (hint, if you've got lots to repair, use an auto-clicker to avoid excessive clicking here)

- junkyard: in '21, all the scrap piles are pre-set and unchanging, just the contents... with '18, the placement is randomised, not to mention around 2-3 times more plentiful... in addition, there's often more cars to be found and salvaged

- cars: in general, '18 has more workshop cars available, but this is only due to how long both games have been out, however I'd consider '21 more in this aspect *if* the developers allowed '18 workshop cars to be imported to '21 - but that hasn't happened yet, so i'll vote '18 for this part as well due to the much much wider range of cars on offer to find in-game (once you subscribe to all the cars you like or are impressed by)

- auction: here, it's hard to say which is better, but certainly '21 would be easier to consider - there's more cars on offer, and you can view cars without the wait time or going through the entire list of cars on offer before bidding on the one you wanted (sometimes it's at the end, so you have to view up to 9 cars prior...).  of course the downside in '21 is that once you're in the auction yard or showcase (depending on which one), you're presented with the chosen car and then a lot of other display cars but you can only properly view the chosen car....

- garage: it's more visually impressive to view a collection of up to 10 cars per garage level, than just viewing one at a time when visiting ('21 only allows viewing 1 at a time)

For anyone who ever took Automotive shop in school, or at a technical school for a voluntary summer course, this program will give you so much confidence, and give you a sense of personal empowerment, to take apart, and rebuild a vehicle you enjoy. Even though this doesn't capture every single aspect, which would be a daunting task for any programmer, it covers many of the essentials to get a car, or truck functional. If there was anything out there for a simulator that could be used in virtual learning, that could produce an in-demand career, ASE certification, or give the recreational hobbyist genuine help, it would be Car Mechanic Simulator 2018.

Pros:
It simplifies the process of vehicle restoration, to give the player a sense of what it could be, without the hours of grinding with an electric sander, using a silica blaster, or painstaking body work with hammer, and Bondo™. Although, it would pose a more interesting challenge in VR to do so, I think I can hold off breathing in any more ferrous materials, with putty goop on my hand.

Building the engine with an air ratchet tool makes satisfaction immediate. In real life, using a socket wrench, dropping said socket wrench, then grumbling because you busted a knuckle or cried a river of man tears trying to retrieve socket wrench among all the sharp, pointed edges crafted by engineers who got their degree at Teufort. I love that air ratchet, and would endorse that it is as easy as the game makes it. Having one with what you build in your garage is a blessing.

WORKSHOP: The content creators bring soul to what they make. I could list 3 of my favorites, but to be fair, go look in the workshop for yourself. These are the magicians that brew the best ballin' rides, whip up the best whips, and conjure the crunkest money hustlers. If anyone ever comes up with a Generation ten Cadillac Eldorado, base, and touring coupe package, I will play with it the rest of the year.

Cons:
Gaskets. I've had to change them on a woeful amount of water pumps, at least one fuel pump, valve covers, 4 barrel & 2 barrel carbs. The kids need to know that without the gaskets, things leak, build pressure, and even explode in my unfortunate experience. It's not hard, remove a bad gasket, clean & prep the metal surface, apply gasket sealant to the new gasket, evenly place new gasket to part.

Even though I bought it because I really wanted to play it and kne what it is, this one is hard to recommend.

Pros:

+ Very detailed and realistic, id say its about 60-70% accurate in comparison to reality. (I am a mechanic myself)

+You learn a lot about cars 

+ If you're a car enthusiast, or simply likes to remove and remount parts, you'll love this game.

+ Expansions like paintshop, bigger garage with more vehicle-lifts and junkyard+barns is very good update from CMS 15.

Cons:
- Demanding game, barely getting steady Frames even on optimal settings.

- That "shopping" list is somewhat useless, what I do myself is take picture with my phone on the list provided after you found everything wrong, and then go to the shop. It would be better if all parts you needed automatically adds into list then you just simply go to shop when you're finished removing all bad parts, but maybe thats part of the challenge. 

- Takes a long time to finally get your paintshop, and all good skill-tree upgrades. Currently level 27 after around 30 hours of gameplay, need level 30 for paintshop. But this also is a good think because it would get boring way too fast like in CMS 15. And that brings me to my other con, which is that the game gets boring after you've done everything you can, but that is also part of Single-Player games. Maybe a future DLC coming with something interesting? 

Do I recommend this game? Absolutely, its a must have for every car enthusiast and car mechanic out there. Very reasonable priced aswell.

So... Is it worth it..? 
  
After a metric ton of bug fixing with 1/2 a ton more to go, yes IMO. 
  
Don't be fooled by the title, Simulator is a stretch. It's more like a SIMPLulator. Every car uses the same Clutch assembly. There isn't an Automatic to be seen. There's one set of pads, one style of Caliper. All of the parts for the cars are pretty standardized and interchange quite a bit between many makes and models. While it makes Brake work way to easy, the game does a really nice job of weaving them into some nice representations of suspension systems and engines. The DLCs introduce more variations and more specific parts per manufacturer which is nice.
  
Though daunting at first if you've never looked at a car apart, it doesn't take long to get going. For me, the game is too simple having done all of this for real in past lives. For the novice, it's a good complexity without being overwhelming. It's enough to be engaging and create complex enough puzzles that demand some investigation. You get a decent warm fuzzy when you finally figure it out. 
  
Leveling up is grindy, but not in a bad way. If anything you level up too quickly. That's one of the game's issues for me, as all that's left once you top out is to collect all the electronic matchboxes. To others, this is actually fun, so I can't really say it's a fault. There is fun to be had even now swapping wheels and painting to make some nice looking rides, and there's plenty of garage space available to store them. The coming Tuning DLC looks to expand on that so it won't be getting any worse than it is for sure.
  
The game includes a "modding" tool that allows you to make all sorts of variants of the cars in game. It's truly brilliant if you have ever wanted to mod something but have no idea what to do. You won't be making a car from scratch in Blender, but you can make a 4WD Vette clone if you want. Basically any car or part in game can be mixed and matched together to create different models/tiers of the cars in game. Like swapping that anemic straight 6 for a supercharged V-8 for example. At level 55 now, this is something that should burn many an hour for me as I make my own matchboxes to play with.
  
The game does have it's issues. The part listing, ordering and inventory systems are great for one at a time use. But trying to do or be anything like a real shop with any kind of inventory is a real hassle. While the main navigation is good, this whole side of the UI is clunky and awkward at best. The game really needs some TLC here if it's ever going to outgrow it's niche status.
 
The grahics are OK. AA is horrible, but it's not really finished yet. It's pretty enough, but no where near many of the top games out in the last few years. Hopefully we'll see some real improvement and optimization here. It makes little sense to me to have a game full of pretty cars and then have to take the game's word for it because an N64's graphics look better...
  
There are still bugs that need ironing out. My experience hasn't been one of game breaking lose everything issues, but there are some who do. Too early to tell who's side of the game these belong to yet. There are still car bugs that need ironing out. Still UI issues in the corners. Still things that can be done to make the game more user friendly.
  
Be warned the forums for the game can really get negative. There have been promises made and delays. The initial launch was bad at best. As it stands now there are DLCs coming, the Jeep paid DLC and a free Tuning DLC. Because delays and quiet for days at a time, people get antsy and angry. It's not unwarranted, things *could* be better.
  
At the end of the day I'm 160 hours in and have had a very good experience. Well worth the price I paid for it. If everything in future goes as well, I'll be playing for a good while yet. Cheers..!

EDIT: As of the 23rd of October the Jeep DLC is released as well a new patch. And a hot patch. And another hot patch. And now we're awaiting a 1.4.3 because there are two big game issues that are messing with people. 
  
I guess you can take that two ways... It's great they continue to patch aggressively. It's not so great 2 major game play bugs were left alone for a few days (the weekend, to be fair) while the forum threads about them multiplied like rabbits. 
  
What I'm looking for now is attention to game play aspects. UI, Controls, the Inventory System. These need some love. As do the graphics, particularly AA and lighting.
  
Still a title worth buying and losing a few hundred hours to...

First off, anyone who has purchased this game as at least looked at or has played CMS 2015. Now there are a lot of negative reviews floating around at the current time, but if you look at the dicussion boards for CMS 2018; you'll notice that the developers are doing their absolute best to resolve issues and get things patched up as quickly as possible to make CMS 2018 game a few hundred times better than CMS 2015. 

There's a lot of things you can do with the game, barn finds, junk yard, repairs of course, rebuilds, etc. Pretty much anything that you could do in CMS 2015, you can do in CMS 2018. But Red Dot has definitely added a hell of a lot more features than there originally were.

10/10 would be frustrated again.

I can't really tell you what it is. Minor issues (at this point) and some minor annoyances with some of the game mechanics aside, the game's fun. 

It's not the type of game you play because you're looking to "win". It's maybe just that sort of straight forward mix of a love for cars and tinkering combined with the simple task of getting a job done.

Assuming you've never played on of the series before, you're given a basic garage. A lot of details abound but most of it is just dressing. You've got a lift, a computer (or tablet in this edition so you don't have to run around as much) and some basic tools to work on tires, shocks and diagnose problems.

There's a map with various locations that unlock as you progress through a fairly linear skill tree. The skill tree improves your speed (doing your work, moving around, etc.), equipment and additional space unlocks (more lifts, paint booth, parking levels to store cars, etc.) as well as some skill improvements (improved repair success).

You have effectively two ways to get a car to work on: they stream in via a series of pending orders you can accept or you can find them in various places on the map. There's the dealership where you can buy a brand new car (for the sake of getting a rare car or a new car to tune), an auction where you can bid on used cars in various shapes but all running, and a junkyard and random barns where you can find old parts and run down (not running) cars to restore.

Once in your garage, you can run cars through the path test to check brakes and suspension, use tools on the engine to check their statuses, etc. Nothing fancy just run the tool and get a result. From there, it's up to you to either diagnose the problem with a order brought in or to just fix that junker you bought at the junkyard. 

The game highlights parts you can remove or place so you don't need to be a mechanic really to know what you're doing. The interface uses a radial menu to change modes, access your inventory and access tools like your tablet to order parts. You can effectively tear down the engine, suspension and transmission and pop them wheels off. You can then repair the parts (depending on your skill and the state of the part), buy replacements and rebuild everything. Or for orders, you can just find the parts that need to be fixed, make sure their status meets the minimum requirement for the job (e.g. some older cars can get parts that are at 50% health so you can offload some of those cheap parts you found at the junkyard and turn a profit), and get paid.

You get XP with each part you remove (+ 1 per part which is super slow but then you tend to take off a lot of parts) and you get larger bundles of XP for jobs (on the order of hundreds of XP). That XP levels you up and grants you a skill point for that skill tree as well as causing a barn to pop up on the map with parts and cars to be bought and restored.

Eventually you can level up enough to unlock the paint booth and dyno where you can paint cars and tune engines (with the DLC), respectively (as well as get a welder to repair bodies and interior cleaning setup to clean up interiors). 

All in all, it's a fun ride. At times, the orders drag on a bit but there's a decent variety of cars (a mix of fake brands with DLC providing real car maker models lilke Ford and Dodge. 

There are minor annoyances. Previously, there were much larger issues and bugs but these days those are fewer and far between. There's still a decent lag issue when accessing an inventory with a decent number of parts. It's annoying buy you deal with it since everything else tends to work. 

Personally, I have my own (short) list of things that bother me. Barns appear with each level but are gone once you loot them of goodies. I haven't reached the end of the skill tree yet (getting there at 30) but I worry that one of the most fun aspects for me (digging around and finding parts to repair and use on restores) is so limited. You have the junkyard, no doubt, but I dunno. I feel limited. 

At times the jobs can get tedious and annoying. Removing valve rods from a v8 gets super annoying fast. Having to take apart an entire engine to find some damned part that didn't come up with any of the tools because, well, there's no way to measure a piston ring or a rubber bearing. Things like that.

My biggest gripe right now is the Auction House. This unlocks after a few levels. You paid a small fee ($200) and get a random assortment of cars in working condition but with varying levels of condition (1 to 5 stars). If you know your cars or eventually unlock a skill that tells you what the average price is of a car, you'll have a sense for just how far to bid. Not too big a deal. But the other bidders are AI...bad AI. It's just like they're a random roll that eventually stop well after the bidding is past the value of the car fully restored. It's rare to get anything below average in terms of price. I sort of don't see the point. You might as well just set it up as a used car dealership and say here are the prices at average price + 20%. Someone  suggested giving the AI limited funds so they can maybe win a car or two but otherwise might put themselves out of the running for certain cars for one reason or another. I think that might be a great solution. 

Despite all this, I've got to say, it's a fun game to play. It's the kind of game you play because you want to just spend a bunch of time tinkering with cars but don't have the money or skills or time to do so in real life. You can test drive the cars, collect some, and just tinker away. Fun times. At $20 it's a great deal, though if you're interested in the name brand car DLCs, I'd definitely wait for a sale to pick everything you want up for $20 or less. Or just get the game and buy the DLC later to reinvigorate the game for you.

Pro's
- Mod support/workshop allows for a huge number of vehicles (of varying quality depending on the modder)
- Same semi-addicitve gameplay of CMS 2015
- Has (slowly) updated and introduced new features, including several DLC packs for new offical cars which have been reletively cheap at around 5$ a pop

Con's
- Almost feels like 2 games, first chunk is spent fixing cars for customers to level up your garage, this segment can feel qutie tedious as things like faster bolt removal are an unlock and you cannot do many of the games other features such as painting etc until later on. - Features present in CMS 2015 such as engine swapping are only just making their way into this game and are still severly underused by both offical cars and mod cars
- Most of your "upgrades" for performance are just shiny versions of regular parts, that add more HP to your car, which you cannot really appreciate as the driving experience as previously mentioned stinks
- Want to change whats under the hood?  Better hope you picked up a model with a turbo or supercharger already installed because otherwise you are out of luck, no changing whats under the hood other than replacing a limited number of parts with shinier "performance" options. This has changed a tiny bit with engine swaps finally being introduced,  however the number of cars this is implemented on remains limited and this still only gives you the option to use premade engine variants. 
- This game has suffered from continuous peformance issues and a number of bugs, I cannot faults the dev's for problems with Mods, however some sort more robust back up is definitly needed, I have repeatedly have a vehicle bug while in parking storage only to lose all the cars on that level.
- Want to see your car collection, get prepared to see only 12 at a time, only to have to load screen back to your garage to then jump to the next 12 cars, no transfering directly between. Also STILL no way to efficently organize cars in the parking garage.
- One of my biggest gripes is probably the fact you cannot easily obtain a car you want. Wish to purchase a new or used car through ANY source in the game? Be prepared to load in and out of the junkyard, auction, or dealer repeatedly while hoping the car you want/need will randomly be there next time. Maybe this is not as much of an issue if only playing the base game but add some cars from the workshop and this becomes a huge headache.  

I only hope that if they make a sequel that some of these aspects are fixed.

October 2021 Update: Don't buy CMS2015; buy Car Mechanic Simulator 2021. It fixes almost every issue I had with CMS2018, particularly the terrible performance. All of the praise I gave CMS2015, better loading times, more subparts, more (non-licensed) cars, etc, all apply to CMS2021 as well when compared to CMS2018.

Original review continues below:

Summary: If you own CMS2015, then the larger amount of content and quality of life improvements are fantastic. But the levelling is far worse than CMS2015. 
For new players, this is where to enter the series. It has a number of the DLC packs for the last game built-in and numerous QoL improvements.

You repair cars. You restore cars. You can drive those in four closed areas (more on the Workshop) with a wonky handling model. That's about all you can do in this game.
I haven't encountered any of the stability issues mentioned in the other reviews. Maybe I've just not played enough. 

Compared to CMS 2015, CMS2018 is an overall improvement in experience. Loading Times are massively improved. All of the non-licensed cars from CMS2015 are included (Even the DLC ones, except the Maluch), with some new ones thrown in. Many parts now have sub-parts, increasing complexity. The engine stand is a sorely-needed addition, meaning you no longer need to keep lifting and dropping the car to strip the engine. Part Repair is no longer a garbage Xcom or Bloodbowl 2-esque diceroll that proudly lies about your success chance. 

The positives aside, I have two huge criticisms that nearly completely outweigh the improvements: The glacial levelling system and the Consolised UI.

Levels in CMS 2015 increased every 1000XP. You got 1XP for each part you took off, put on, examined or repaired. You got 100XP for completing a job. You also unlocked all the skills by around Level 15 provided that you hadn't unlocked any customisation options. 
Levels in CMS2018 increase on a sliding scale. Early levels take less XP and later levels take more. You only gain XP for taking parts off, putting them on and for completing jobs; Examining and repairing parts no longer gives any XP. There are more skills, but all of them are locked behind level targets. For example, you have to be at least level 35 to unlock Body Part Repair.
Workshop expansions return form CMS2012, however certain tools are locked behind those Workshop expansions. You can't repair car chassis until Level 30, since that's when you unlock the Workshop expansion that the Welder is hidden in.
I'm 42 hours in at time of writing and I've only just unlocked it. I still can't repair body parts though.
In CMS2015, you could do both things by Level 5, about four hours in, if you really wanted to.
The early levels are cluttered with useless skills like +10% movement speed and 5% better income on jobs, while you can only improve your repair chance by 10% every 5 levels.

The UI is a sidewards step from CMS2015. It went from a UI entirely based on hotkeys to one nearly entirely based on a console-derived right-click radial menu. This menu doesn't always register input, several times I've had to re-open it and re-select my option for it to work, usually when trying to open the Inventory or the Job Summary. 
Nearly all of the hotkeys have been stripped out. The Job Summary hotkey (I) is gone. The Mode hotkeys (1, 2 and 3) are gone. The Diagnosis Tool hoykeys (F1, F2 and F3) are gone. The only one left, for the Tablet (T), doesn't work in the Interior modes; you have to switch back to Body Part disassembly for the Tablet hotkey to work again. The options to switch beteen assembly and disassembly move around the radial menu like they're playing a game of Musical Chairs. The Diagnosis tools are only accessible from the Disassembly mode ([i]not[/i] from the Examination mode) and only from the Right-Click menu, where they're hidden under their own option.
The parts list, while a good idea, is completely useless since you can't add a part from disassembly mode or remove things from it from the Tablet or Computer. You still have to quickly open the tablet, search for the part and buy it before you forget which part you need. Wheels and Tyres are the worst, since you now have to remember the Size, ET, Profile, Width and style of both the Tyre and Wheel.

There's a few other annoyances, but they're not really worth mentioning.

Even with these issues, I do still recommend CMS2018 over CMS2015. But there's still room for improvement.

I don't normally leave reviews but having been enticed by the overall rating of this game I think it needs knocking down a peg. Have played 17 hours at review time so should be long enough to make a judgement:

The good:
-The house music radio station is banging
-Probably teaches you about cars if you know literally zero

The bad:
-Core game is wildly unrealistic in almost every way I can think of:
*Part prices are way off
*Many orders are nonsensical - rusty BoS comes in with 200k miles on the clock wanting a full engine, gearbox and suspension rebuild costing 10x what the car is worth
*Minimal to no electronics - no wiring looms, plugs etc despite this being an ever bigger part of modern cars. Why is the ABS module the only module - where are all the CPUs - engine management one being most obvious? Many garage jobs involve changing sensors - there are none in this game.
*No way you would put a car on a track and be able to work out which bush or brake component isnt working
*Despite worn parts showing as rusty, rust does not seem to impact disassembly. Having spent 4 hour trying to remove 2 of the part they call the outer tie rod on a 16 year old car, in game this is overlooked. Equally you can have a part that's new out the box or nearly new that's faulty but not here
*Bolts, tools and the general assembly of cars is very minimal but thats pretty much all you deal with when working on cars for real. 3 toolboxes in this garage and not a spanner in sight. Working out which tool is best to use to reach an unreachable bolt is usually half the challenge
-Struggling to see the point - race track but no racing, test track not customisable for different tests. You can restore a car but to what end? No place to use it.
-Driving physics are weird af. Healthy cars have such bizarre handling and as for damaged cars - If I have 'sway bar links' with 1% health with springs and shocks that need replacing, shouldn't my car wallow like a boat in a storm?
-As a brit the part names do my head in. Anti-Roll Bar, Wing (body panel), Bonnet. English language option would be nice!
-Sub categories are a mess. Air filter should be under 'intake' the exhaust manifold should be under exhaust', clutch is not part of the gearbox so should be called drivetrain as should drive shafts which they call suspension, orders mention 'running gear' - wtf is running gear? Do I find it next to the yoga leggings?
-Repairs - parts that can be repaired IRL cannot in game and vice versa
-Engine oil just falls out the car when I ask it to and all cars get filled up with the same stuff. What happened to gearbox oil, bleeding the brakes, where is the air con system for that matter? 
-No engine or gearbox mounts. Gearbox just comes off in game but a gearbox is really heavy and you always use a stand, lift or jack to assist you
-Engine either runs or doesn't - since when? Blown headgasket, misfire, timing is off, damaged piston crown are all times when the engine runs just not well.

Probably loads of other things I've noticed and not mentioned. Overall the gameplay is quite boring, very grindy and repetitive, I would rate it's realism at 30% or less. As a simulator it's rubbish, and it's not much fun as a game with objectives or achievements. I don't get it, and nor should you.

Now to what I like and dislike about the game

[h1] Positives [/h1]
- Variety of different cars to work on (Modern, Classic, Muscle/Exotic etc.)

- Actually, have to "grind" to get levels, money, and upgrade points (Takes longer to get certain things so IMO, once you actually get what you've been grinding for -  e.g. Enough money for a full restoration project - then you feel more appreciation for it)

But then you could get a hard build where you get one piece of information and then have to work the rest out for yourself. This obviously adds a bit of skill to the game which makes it less boring)

- A lot of different varieties to choose from when restoring cars (A lot of different customisations to choose from whether it be a custom engine or spraying the car a different colour)

[h1] Negatives [/h1]
- Car problems given by the Owner do not match when test driving (e.g. if the owner comes in and says their car moves to the left when driving, it doesn't do that when you take it for a test drive - I know this may not bother people but I'm just pointing it out)

- No option/key binding to hide the entire UI (I like taking screenshots and even though there is no UI when using the Photo feature inside the Garage, I would like to actually get better shots when using the Car outside on the test track or the Airport for e.g. but because I can't hide the UI the speedometer still shows)

[h1] Final Review [/h1]
Other than what I've already stated, I have no problem with the game so far. It has it's problems but they can all be solved with an easy fix. The game has nice cars, cool features and I enjoy playing it. At this moment in time I haven't purchased any DLC and according to the reviews I don't think im going to. Exactly what it says on the tin. Possibly the best take-it-apart-and-put-it-back-together-until-it-works simulator now in my Steam library.

Good:
* The main assembly and disassembly interfaces are great and lend themselves well to keyboard-and-mouse play. 
* Good combination of puzzles in the main game and good written descriptions that hint you towards the source of each problem within those puzzles.
* Good procedurally generated sidequests in the main "story" mode. These offer a good balance of complexity and challenge level aside from the main quests.
* Fixing up junkers and hunting for parts in abandoned barns is exactly as fun as it should be.
* Good search interface for buying new parts, with "Noodel" search and the internal storefronts hitting the 90s look and feel (and also, instantaneous shipping, which I wish were a real thing).
* Forgetting to drain the oil pan is accurately represented in game (and has an achievement).

Bad:
* Soulless presentation emblematic of many "simulator" titles. The art assets are good, and the game does what it wants to do, but only that at this writing.
* Tutorial needs a significant revamp. At this writing, it's easy to get trapped in it thinking you're playing the main game and gaining experience and items, only to lose all progress once you visit the test track and fade to black. Oddly, achievements work inside of it, too.
* Level-up system that restricts interface options after demonstrating them to the player. Especially true for folks that boot into the game for the first time after noodling with the tutorial and wonder where the tablet interface disappears to.
* Ghosts of screws are very visible through a part, while hidden or internal parts do not always appear, leading to frustration when something isn't coming off for no visual reason. A flyout warning when something can't be disassembled and a visual cue would be useful.
* Damage level on parts is almost always represented by visual surface corrosion, making some of the advanced testing parts (OBD, voltage tester, path tests, etc) less useful than they would otherwise be.
* Not terribly accessible outside of keyboard and mouse play, due to the CAD-like features of assembly and disassembly.

Dubious:
* The arc welder's safety instructions appear to be the instructions for an electric tea kettle.

I usually wait until I beat a game to write a review for it, but this is not exactly a game that one "beats" in the traditional sense. CMS2018 is exactly what it says it is: You take the role of yourself, starting with a small humble garage with a single car lift, and just about $4,000 to your name. It takes me back to my youth of Snap-Ons Gearhead Garage (http://www.gearheadgarage.com/).

I grabbed this on a sale and I think I paid around $10 for it, and it's worth every penny. The game is really separated into a few smaller meta-games.

On one hand, you've got your phone orders; these are customers that need help with their cars. Obviously as the game starts off you do things like perform basic brake service, changing oil and filters, and very minor improvements. On the other hand; you've got complete car restorations. I mean sex is great and all, but have you bought an old rusted 1962 AC Cobra from an old barn and restored it to 100% of it's former glory with a complete rebuild and then turned around and sold it for a tidy $80K profit?

As you complete jobs, you earn experience and you level up, which provides you with talent points you can use to do things like move faster, unscrew things quicker, and even expand your garage. The expansion of the garage is the most satisfying thing as it often results in unlocking other great features, like the engine pulling crane, the battery charger, and eventually the interior detail shop or the body shop/paint shop.

I have only put about 23 hours into CMS2018 and I feel satisfied with my purchase. The game is enjoyable. It's a zen garden but with bolts and rust instead of plants. It's a fun way to wind down after a stressful day at work.

I will admit, the game is not without it's flaws: The music is terrifyingly bad (in my own opinion) and there is some strange UI lag from time to time. There is also an unreasonable painful grind to get to level 30 (the level in which you unlock the body and paint shop). I often found myself finishing every single order I could as quickly I as I could, regardless of what the customer wanted - even if it meant doing the most bare minimum, JUST to get the XP.

But even with the minor faults, the game is fun and worth the cost. Go out there and fix up some cars!

After playing for some time, I feel that this game doesn't remotely deserve its average rating. Multiple aspects of this game are highly unrealistic, and there are various bugs, and things that just make no sense. I'm not convinced that mechanics were involved in any way with the creation of this game. At best, they were car nerds. Furthermore, this is a total dlc farm with 15 paid dlc and counting. Altogether, these dlc cost around 4x what this game is worth.

The tutorial is so worthless it shouldn't be called a tutorial. The only question it covers is "what is in the shop?" with very few hints of how to even use said items. Despite this, the player needs to figure out how to repair and test drive one of the two cars present. The game fails to mention that you won't be able to repair or drive one of them with your limited funds. More importantly, it fails to clearly tell you how to fix the car that you actually can fix. I didn't make it out of the tutorial without consulting google. If a random person online can easily tell me how the tutorial zone works, you'd think that the devs might be capable of such a task in their own handcrafted tutorial. As you continue the game, you will learn why this was too great a challenge for said devs.

Players are forced to be downright insane about replacing ONLY the "broken" positions with new parts. This means that if you have 4 spark plugs and 3 need replacing, you replace the worst 3 but put the one of the new parts into a slot that wasn't broken, this doesn't count as fixed. You will be forced to switch around parts to make sure that slot 1, 2, and 4 have new parts and slot 3 has the old, but still perfectly functional part. You better hope you caught your mistake early or you will spend the next 10 minutes unscrewing and removing pieces that "get in the way" (sometimes even realistically) of reaching the spark plugs for the pointless swap.

Multiple parts are just buggy with absolutely no obvious reason why you can reach them from some positions, but not from others. Looking especially at the damn starters that force you to guess whether they "need" to be reached from the engine bay, or from below. This is pretty much a 50/50 guess as there's absolutely no logic to it.

A lot of parts present in modern cars just don't exist in this game at all, particularly electrical ones.

For some reason, the max shop level can only be reached after performing around a million jobs that are virtually identical. How many V8 OHV Gearboxes do I have to replace before I become "experienced" enough for my shop to upgrade? way, way, way too many. Why shop components and diagnostic tools are based on experience instead of money is a total mystery and far from immersive. In fact, there's nothing immersive about the core mechanics :P of this game at all.

This game is just petty when it forces you to remove 4 "clip" parts individually to reach a part you're actually trying to remove. Oh, and they each have individual quality and might need replacing. This is just an example of how monotonously dull this game so quickly becomes.

Whenever a license plate needs replacing, you're going to need to memorize the plate number/letter combination, including spaces, as well as the plate type. There's a system for making a so-called "shopping list"; however, it's almost entirely useless because it leaves out details such as plate numbers and other key details that keep you from wasting your money, and especially time, on the wrong parts. The shopping list system is actually so useless that using is a total waste of time.

There are far more issues I haven't bothered to mention, but they all pretty much add up to make this game get very old extremely fast. No fully released game should end up like this. If this was their first title in the car mechanic simulator series then it might be more understandable why they left so many problems in the game, but it is not.

If you want a brief and incomplete introduction to the anatomy of a car, you can get all of that with the base game in a mere couple of hours. After that, the game loses most of its value as anything beyond a time-waster.

This game takes place in a world where all of the car manufacturers use the same parts, center-lock wheels don't exist, and cars only get rusted rather than the usual damages. The game is fun, but not overly realistic. You get the experience of picking parts and fixing cars, but some of the deeper aspects are missing. There's no torquing bolts, managing wiring, or checking fluids that aren't oil. In some areas, the order that you remove/add parts is pretty unrealistic and all damage is rendered as rust regardless of the source. The game also has some customization, but its a bit limited.

That said, the game is pretty relaxing. The game skips the more mundane parts of mechanic work and lets you enjoy the fun parts of the job. The DLC is also pretty good. The cars in the base game are decent, but the DLC adds a lot of variety and character. Its always satisfying to finish a car and drive it around one of the test areas. If you're looking for a serious car simulator, this isn't it, but if you love cars and want to relax or kill time, this game is perfect.

Oh, and be sure to use your own music for the radio and turn down the volume. This game loves loud, obnoxious music.

As much as I want to like this, particularly with how much time I spent with CMS15, the new version got more kludgy, not less. It feels like their goal with the new version was to see how much minutia they could add, rather than how to make it feel more like working on a car.

The UI is pretty kludgy, too, with the ability to put parts you want to buy on a list, but, when you open the list, it obscures part of the list of parts in the store, making it so you'd have to open and close the parts list pretty often. i love this game. It is an easy way to learn about the inner workings of your car and is fairly easy to play.

I like it.  Despite a few very frustrating issues in certain spots.  And, despite the repetetive nature of its activities.


I didn't expect to enjoy it as much as I do, actually.  I thought it would be fun and interesting, and maybe educational in a way.  Which it is all of those.  Mostly interesting and fun to build a wreck up to something special.  There's something that is satisfying about seeing all that shiny clean metal!

I would have liked to see more body and perfromance mods, but it still has plenty of other parts to work with.  Spoilers, scoops, and other body kits.  I enjoy customizing vehicles like that in games.  You can't pull out one engine and put in another, either.  It has to be the exact same construction. You can replace some standard parts with performance versions, but it seemed fairly limited in that it didn't really change the systems, it is just the same model with a different texture and better attributes that apply to the cars handling on the track(s).

I like how you can sit in the car and look around inside, even start it up.  One more addition to that would be great, to be able to modulate the throttle while sitting there, so you can hear the engine and exhaust systems.  That's part of the fun of doing mechanic things like this, isn't it?

That said, I am no actual mechanic and have not done a lot of actual work on vehicles beyond some basic things.  This game does simplify it enough to bring it into my realm, but also seems to give you a kind of "feel" that you are building or working on a car.  It's not really "sim" in that you have to crawl under, get your hands greasy, or have a tough time reaching down into an engine bay, etc.  In fact, you can actual adjust the camera enough to see inside of, say, the engine itself, without dismantling it.

And, the way the game shows that a part needs repair is through the amount of "rust" it shows.  No breaks, tears, leaks, burns, punctures, etc.  So, its' not a matter of actually trying to diagnose things as you might in real life.  It has a definite pattern that over time you come to realize, and can then speed things up a bit.  But, at that point, it becomes kinduva a brainless game that you can play just to waste time not having to think about things.  Which is sometimes good, sometimes not.

There are some things you can do to be the detective to figure out an issue on a car that involves some actual thinking, but, it's not really necessary most of the time, especially after you get all the level perks to help diagnose things.

So, those are some good and general points about the game.  There are a couple nuisances, however.  I find that working with tires, and shocks tend to slow my workflow way down.  So much that I avoid doing them, unless I really have to.  That may be just me, I don't know.

The worst thing, however, is its inventory system.  While the User Interface looks very nice, it actually has two MAJOR issues.

1) Despite the beautiful design, actually USING the inventory/warehouse dialog windows is horrendous!  There is no way to use the keybaord to scroll/navigate through the MANY MANY parts, leaving me to use a very tedious mouse-wheeling until I get to the ONE particular part I want.  And then, if I accept that part, even if I am looking for the very next  item in the list, I have to scroll allllll over again!  Horrible.  It desperately needs "stacking" or some other way of organizing these parts. 

2) If that design was not enough, the code, database, or memory management of the inventory system is horrendous, as well.  Because every time I bring up the dreaded inventory panel, I can count on waiting a long while for it to come up, my (quite powerful) PC heats up and the fans start whirring fast under the load.  And, even after you close the panel, after that point, the game struggles to do most things that it was doing fine, before.  Definitely buggy in here.

Great car mechanic simulator for people who are interested in learning the basics of car mechanical repair. It doesn't cover everything about car repair and maintenance such as how to do brake and fuel lines.

This game is hard for me to recommend but also hard to thumbs down.  I enjoyed repairing and rebuilding cars, but there are a lot of annoying bugs.  

For instance when repairing cars lets say you remove 4 pistons and 2 are bad.  You buy 2 new pistons and replace the four.  Put the whole care back together to see it tell you you haven't fixed the bad piston.  It's because you have to put the new one in the same slot as the bad one.  I tried several methods to mediate this ridiculously impactful bug, like only taking off half the suspension at a time.  But for parts that lie together like pistons and crankshafts it can be very frustrating.

I am pretty close to being able to completely rebuild and ignore the repair jobs, but this ruins some of the vlaue for me of roleplaying a repair shop that does restorations.

I have to assume that the dev team has received this feedback, perhaps they will fix it.  I don't know.  but for now I"m going to put it on the shelf and reluctantly thumbs it down.
